name: Near Absolute Zero Temps
subject: quantum-computing
subjectTitle: A Skeptic's Guide to Quantum Computing

lesson.title: Ten Millikelvin: Colder Than Deep Space
lesson.summary: Superconducting quantum chips typically operate around ten to twenty millikelvin, colder than the vacuum of deep space, because that is roughly what basic thermodynamics demands to keep thermal noise from disturbing the qubits.
lesson.body:
To make the cryogenic cooling requirement concrete, it helps to look at the actual numbers involved. The coldest stage of a dilution refrigerator holding a superconducting quantum chip typically operates around ten to twenty millikelvin, that is, roughly one hundredth of one degree above absolute zero. For comparison, the cosmic microwave background radiation that fills the vacuum of deep space sits at about 2.7 kelvin, meaning the inside of a quantum computer's refrigerator is routinely colder than the empty space between galaxies, by more than a factor of one hundred.

The reason the target has to be this extreme comes directly from basic thermodynamics. A superconducting qubit's operating energy, the gap between its computational states, corresponds to a temperature on the order of a fraction of a kelvin to a few kelvin, depending on the qubit's design. For thermal noise in the environment to avoid randomly kicking the qubit out of its intended state, the surrounding temperature needs to sit well below that energy scale, so that the probability of a stray thermal excitation is negligible rather than merely small. Millikelvin temperatures push that thermal excitation probability down close to the practical limits of current refrigeration technology, which is why this specific regime, and not some more moderate cold temperature, is the target.

Reaching and holding these temperatures is itself a nontrivial physics and engineering feat. Dilution refrigerators achieve millikelvin cooling using the physics of mixing two isotopes of helium, helium-3 and helium-4, which, when cooled and diluted into each other in a particular way, absorb heat from their surroundings as they mix, similar in spirit to how evaporating sweat cools skin, but exploiting a quantum-mechanical difference between the two isotopes rather than ordinary evaporation. It is one of only a small number of technologies capable of reaching and sustaining temperatures in this range continuously, for the days or weeks a quantum computing experiment might run.

It is also worth remembering that absolute zero itself is unreachable in principle, a consequence of the third law of thermodynamics, so millikelvin temperatures are not a stepping stone toward some lower target but close to the practical floor of what refrigeration can achieve at all. That the qubit-hosting environment already sits this close to the physical limit of cooling technology is a strong hint that scaling up the number of qubits sharing that environment will run into hard physical constraints, which is exactly the subject of the next few sections.

There is also a subtler point worth making here. Because the system is already operating so close to the coldest temperatures achievable with existing technology, there is very little room to compensate for scaling problems by simply "cooling harder." Unlike many engineering constraints, which can be relaxed by throwing more resources at them, the temperature floor is set by thermodynamics itself, and by how efficiently helium-3 and helium-4 mixing can extract heat. That is a large part of why the qubit count achievable inside a single refrigerator has grown so much more slowly than qubit designs themselves have improved.
